```{r echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(p8105.datasets)
```

## Problem 1

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
data("ny_noaa")
#Data cleaning
ny_df = 
  ny_noaa |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(
    year = year(date),
    month = month(date),
    day = day(date),
    prcp = prcp/10,
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax)/10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin)/10
  )

#Most commonly observed snowfall values
ny_noaa |> 
  group_by(snow) |> 
  summarize(n_obs=n()) |> 
  arrange(desc(n_obs))

#Average max temp in January and July in each station across years
ny_df |> 
  filter(month == 1 | month == 7) |> 
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, color = month))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(color = "red")+
  facet_grid(.~month)
```

In the `ny_noaa` dataset, there are `r ncol(ny_noaa)` columns/variables and a total of `r nrow(ny_noaa)` observations tracking precipitation levels, snowfall, snow depth, maximum and minimum temperatures, and the ID numbers of which weather stations in New York state collected this data. In this dataset, there are `r sum(is.na(ny_noaa))` total `NA` entries, meaning that `r round(mean(is.na(ny_noaa))*100)`% of the total entries in the data set are `NA` values.

After cleaning the dataset, the most commonly observed values are 0 mm with a count of 2,008,508 obs, NA with a count of 381,221 obs, and 25 mm with a count of 31,022 obs. This is most likely due to the fact that New York is a seasonal state with snowfall mostly occurring during the winter season. Since snowfall is uncommon throughout most of the year, there would not be many occurrences of snowfall in this dataset. The large number of NA would also suggest that snowfall was not recorded for every observation. When plotting the average max temperature for January and July across years there seems to be fluctuating shape for the month of January between low and medium temps, while July remains relatively constant at higher temps. There are some outliers for both January and July at lower temperatures. 

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE,  fig.width=12, fig.height=16}
#plot_i and plot_ii
plot_i = 
  ny_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = tmax, y = tmin))+
  geom_hex()

plot_ii = 
  ny_df |> 
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = snow))+
  geom_histogram()+
  facet_wrap(.~year)

(plot_i/plot_ii)+
   plot_layout(heights = c(1, 3))
```

## Problem 2
```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
accel_df = 
  read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv", na = c("", ".", "NA")) |> 
  janitor::clean_names()

covar_df = 
  read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4, na = c("", ".", "NA")) |> 
  janitor::clean_names()

accel_covar = 
  left_join(accel_df, covar_df, by = "seqn") |>
  filter(age >= 21) |> 
  drop_na(sex, age, bmi, education) |> 
  mutate(
    sex = factor(sex,
                 levels = c(1,2),
                 labels = c("Male", "Female")),
    education = factor(education,
                       levels = c(1,2,3),
                       labels = c("Less than high school", "High school equivalent", 
                                  "More than high school"))
  )

#reader-friendly table
education_tb = 
  accel_covar |> 
  count(education, sex) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n
  ) |> 
  knitr::kable()

#age distribution visualization
accel_covar |> 
ggplot(aes(age)) + 
geom_histogram() + 
facet_grid(sex~education)

```

In merging the two nhanes accelerometer and covariate data sets, it was found that among the males in the data, 27 had a Less than high school level education, 35 had a high school equivalent education, and 56 had more than high school education. Among females in the dataset, 28 had a Less than high school level education, 23 had a high school equivalent education, and 59 had more than high school education.

In examining the age distribution across education levels, stratified by sex, for both males and females, there seemed to be older participants that had a Less than high school education (slightly skewed to the left). For a high school equivalent education there is a wide spread of ages with a heavier concentration of older participants among females than males. For an education level that is more than high school there is also a wide distribution of ages for both males and females, where there are younger ages among females (slightly right skewed) compared to males.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
accel_covar |> 
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440, 
    names_to = "time",
    values_to = "activity"
  )|> 
  group_by(seqn, sex, education, age) |> 
  summarise(
    total_activity = sum(activity, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE)+
  facet_grid(.~education)
```

In looking at total activity over the day between education categories and sex, the general trend across all categories and sexes is that as age increases, total activity decreases. Among those with a less than high school education, males remain generally more active through most ages as they get older compared to females, with a peak in activity levels around 60 for both sexes and then a steep decline. Among those with a high schoool equivalent education level, females remain substantially more active than males, especially during the 20-50 age range. Among those with more than a high school education, both male and female activity stay consistent until the age 60 before declining.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
accel_covar |>
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to = "time",
    names_prefix = "min",
    names_transform = list(time = as.numeric),
    values_to = "activity"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    hour = time/60
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = hour, y = activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education)
```

Over a 24-hour activity time course, across all education levels, there is higher levels of activity occurring through the middle of the day (between hours 10 - 15). Between all three education levels, those who had more than high school education had substantially higher levels of activity. Between the sexes, activity levels throughout the 24 hour period coincide closely throughout the day.

## Problem 3
```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
jan2020_df = 
  read_csv("data/Jan 2020 Citi.csv", na = c("", ".", "NA")) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(
    year = "2020",
    month = "January"
  )

july2020_df = 
  read_csv("data/July 2020 Citi.csv", na = c("", ".", "NA")) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
    mutate(
    year = "2020",
    month = "July"
  )

jan2024_df = 
  read_csv("data/Jan 2024 Citi.csv", na = c("", ".", "NA")) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
    mutate(
    year = "2024",
    month = "January"
  )

july2024_df = 
  read_csv("data/July 2024 Citi.csv", na = c("", ".", "NA")) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
    mutate(
    year = "2024",
    month = "July"
  )

citi_df = 
  bind_rows(
    jan2020_df,
    july2020_df,
    jan2024_df,
    july2024_df
  )
```
The data set `citi_df` contains merged data information on rides with a total duration of less than 4 hours in January and July of 2020 and January and July of 2024. The data set has a total of `r ncol(citi_df)`variables containing `r paste(names(citi_df), collapse = ",")`. With a total of `r nrow(citi_df)` ride information across all 4 months.

```{r message = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
citi_df |> 
  group_by(year, month, member_casual) |>
  summarise(
    total_rides = n()
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = total_rides
  ) |> 
  knitr::kable()
```
Based on the results of the table, in January of 2020, there were 984 casual riders and 11,436 member riders, compared to July of 2020 where there were 5,637 casual riders and 15,411 member riders. In January 2024 there were 2,108 casual riders and 16,753 member riders while in July of 2024 there were 10,894 casual riders and 36,262 member riders. 

```{r message = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# 5 most popular starting stations for July 2024
citi_df |> 
  filter(
    month == "July", year == 2024) |> 
  group_by(start_station_name) |> 
  summarise(
    total_rides = n()
  ) |> 
  arrange(desc(total_rides)) |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |> 
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
citi_df |> 
  group_by(month, year, weekdays) |> 
  summarise(
    med_duration = median(duration)
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = weekdays, y = med_duration, color = month))+
  geom_point() + 
  facet_grid(.~year)
```
Based on this plot that looks at the effect of the day of the week on median ride duration for the months of January and July for 2020 and 2024, it can be seen that in 2020, the median ride duration was overall substantially much higher in July than it was in January. In 2024, median ride duration for July is still overall greater than in January, it is to a lesser degree than in 2020. Between 2020 and 2024, the median ride duration for July dropped significantly closer to the median duration in January.

```{r message = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
citi_df |> 
  filter(year == 2024) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = duration, fill = member_casual))+
  geom_histogram() + 
  facet_grid(month~rideable_type)
```
For 2024, the number of electric bikes and the duration on those bikes were on slightly similar levels to duration on classic bikes during January, however, in July, while duration for both bike types increased, distribution remained similar with substantially more electric_bike use for both casual and member riders. In both months and across both bike types the distribution of duration is skewed to the right.
